analysis.one_liner: Requires the Supreme Court to adopt a code of conduct, disclose justices' gifts, and step aside in conflict cases.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring the Supreme Court to adopt a code of conduct and disclose justices' gifts, travel, and income died in the House Judiciary Committee without a vote, despite backing from 161 of 216 House Democrats and none from any House Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Supreme Court to adopt a binding code of conduct for the first time, set up a process for investigating ethics complaints against justices, require public disclosure of gifts, travel, and income given to justices and their clerks, and expand the rules for when a justice must step aside from a case involving someone who gave them money or spent money on their appointment. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary litigants and the public, who would get enforceable ethics rules, a complaint process, and public disclosure of the money and gifts flowing to Supreme Court justices — the same standards that already apply to members of Congress and lower-court judges. Parties to cases would learn when a justice received money or gifts from an opposing party or its allies and could move to disqualify that justice, with a panel of outside judges reviewing the decision.

how_it_helps.text: For the first time, the bill requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for justices within 180 days, with public notice and comment, and to post the rules on a searchable public website — closing the gap that left the justices as the only federal judges without a written ethics code.

It creates a real complaint process: citizens could file ethics complaints against a justice, and a randomly chosen panel of five chief circuit judges would investigate, with subpoena power, and publish its findings.
It requires disclosure rules for justices' gifts, income, and reimbursements at least as strict as the rules that bind members of the House and Senate, and extends them to justices' law clerks.

It expands recusal: a justice must step aside if a party or its affiliate made lobbying contacts or spent substantial funds to support the justice's appointment, or gave the justice, the justice's spouse, or minor child income or gifts within a six-year window — and parties would have to disclose such payments in their briefs, so litigants could see the conflict and ask for a disqualification review by outside judges.
It adds transparency on the outside money that shapes cases: anyone filing an amicus brief would have to name who funded the brief, and the courts would run an annual audit of compliance.

It requires public notice on court websites whenever a judge or justice is disqualified and why, and directs the Federal Judicial Center to study compliance with the disqualification rules and report to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: The justices themselves, who would face an enforceable conduct code, a complaint and investigation process, and expanded disqualification rules for the first time. Also the wealthy patrons, companies, and allied groups that currently pay for justices' travel, gifts, and hospitality and would have to disclose it — and parties and amici in high-stakes cases, who would have to list gifts and funding connected to the justices and to their own briefs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Justices and the donors who fund them

drawbacks.text: The enforcement is partly circular: complaint findings go back to the Supreme Court itself for 'necessary and appropriate action,' so even a supported complaint about a justice would be judged by the same nine justices, and disqualification motions involving a justice are reviewed by the other eight, not an outside panel.

Opponents raise a constitutional objection: Congress has never imposed a conduct code on the justices directly, and critics argue this treads on separation of powers, since the Court would still write the actual rules and could modify its own code later.

Some provisions are broad and could be contested in good faith: a justice must disqualify over any 'lobbying contact' by a party's affiliate and over income or gifts going back six years, and the new disqualification-motion process lets any party force a case to a stop pending review — rules that critics say could be used to shop for judges or stall litigation.
The bill's complaint and audit machinery (panel reports, annual amicus audits, biennial studies) adds administrative burden to the federal court system and the Administrative Office of the Courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — applying to the Supreme Court the same written conduct code, gift disclosure, and recusal standards that already bind members of Congress and every other federal judge — is clear and largely uncontroversial in design, since the bill copies existing frameworks rather than inventing new ones. The main honest costs are the partial self-enforcement loop and the breadth of the new disqualification triggers, which courts and litigants would have to sort out. The bill was never even considered in committee, so none of these design questions were tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress; the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, with Reps. Jerrold Nadler, Mike Quigley, and David Cicilline as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
It eventually drew 161 cosponsors — all Democrats; no House Republican signed on.
The action history shows nothing after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Supreme Court's nine sitting justices are better off, because they remain the only federal judges with no enforceable written ethics code, no complaint process, and gift disclosure only on their own initiative. The donors and litigants who fund justices' travel and appear before them also keep the status quo of no disclosure and broad discretion over recusal.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split entirely by party: 161 of 216 House Democrats signed on, and no House Republican did; the bill also never advanced in the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The bill would end the justices' status as the only federal judges without a binding conduct code, a complaint process, or outside disclosure rules, and would expand when they must step aside from cases. Incumbent officeholders were the direct target of the bill.

industries.industry: Wealthy patrons and litigants who fund justices' travel and hospitality
industries.note: Gifts, income, and reimbursements to justices would have to be disclosed under congressional-level rules, and money given by a party within six years of a case would force disqualification. The bill removes the discretion of these arrangements rather than any fee they pay.

industries.industry: Trade associations and ideological groups that fund amicus briefs
industries.note: They could keep filing briefs but would have to name anyone funding 3% of their revenue or over $100,000, and their filings would face annual audits. Group-backed influence campaigns in major cases would become visible rather than anonymous.
